# Book III, Proposition 26

*Equal angles stand on equal circumferences*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> In equal circles equal angles stand on equal circumferences, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it, in our measure of circumferences · Euclid's argument, with one step changed

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/26-idea.svg" alt="Give the equal circles ABC, DEF equal angles, at the centres G, H (yellow) or at the circumferences, at A and D (blue): the circumferences BKC, ELF they stand on come out equal (red)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Give the equal circles ABC, DEF equal angles, at the centres G, H (yellow) or at the circumferences, at A and D (blue): the circumferences BKC, ELF they stand on come out equal (red).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/III/26.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition III.26, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ABC, DEF be equal circles, and in them let there be equal angles, namely at the centres the angles BGC, EHF, and at the circumferences the angles BAC, EDF;

I say that the circumference BKC is equal to the circumference ELF.

For let BC, EF be joined.

Now, since the circles ABC, DEF are equal,

the radii are equal.

Thus the two straight lines BG, GC are equal to the two straight lines EH, HF;

and the angle at G is equal to the angle at H;

therefore the base BC is equal to the base EF. [I. 4]

And, since the angle at A is equal to the angle at D,

the segment BAC is similar to the segment EDF; [III. Def. 11]

and they are upon equal straight lines.

But similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another; [III. 24]

therefore the segment BAC is equal to EDF.

But the whole circle ABC is also equal to the whole circle DEF;

therefore the circumference BKC which remains is equal to the circumference ELF.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

| | |
|---|---|
| Proof | ✅ Proved |
| Statement | The whole enunciation. Euclid's two cases, each stated on its own, with equal circumferences read as equal in measure and congruent, which says more than Heath's words. |
| Argument | Euclid's, with one step changed. Euclid's argument where the angles at the circumferences are acute; where they are right, BC and EF are diameters, and where obtuse, III.22 passes to the acute angle, as Heath proposes (vol. 2, p. 57). The remainders are equal in measure by Euclid's subtraction, and congruent by III.24 applied to the remaining segments, since a congruence cannot be subtracted. |
| Representation | "Equal circumferences" is read as equal in measure and congruent (`Arc.Congruent`), the congruence through Common Notion 4, as circumferences that coincide. So "in equal circles" does real work: in unequal circles equal angles give equal measures, but no congruence. The centres G and H are given, as the enunciation speaks of angles at the centres. |
| Reviewed | The statement and the argument read against Heath's text, for every departure from Euclid, at commit [`dcb1767`](https://github.com/jackChallis/stoicheia/commit/dcb1767) ([the record](../../review/III/26.toml)) |

Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where a lemma does a step Euclid takes for granted and where a step is argued another way; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Argued another way.** "therefore the base BC is equal to the base EF." Given the angles at A and D, the Lean sorts them as acute, right or obtuse: if right, BC and EF are diameters, each two radii; if obtuse, III.22 passes to the acute angle in the other segment.
- **Done by `Prop24.equalMeasure`.** "therefore the segment BAC is equal to EDF." III.24 makes the segments BAC, EDF congruent, and its companion `Prop24.equalMeasure` gives what Euclid takes with them: their circumferences are equal in measure.
- **Argued another way.** "therefore the circumference BKC which remains is equal to the circumference ELF." The remainders BKC, ELF are equal in measure by Euclid's subtraction [C.N. 3]. Their congruence cannot come by subtraction: it comes from III.24 applied to the remaining segments, which are similar, their angles making two right angles with the equal angles at A and D [III. 22].

```lean
/-- In equal circles equal angles stand on equal circumferences, whether they stand at the centres
or at the circumferences. -/
theorem Prop26 {A B C D E F G H K L : Point} {ABC DEF : Circle} (hcircles : EqualCircles ABC DEF)
    (hG : Centre G ABC) (hH : Centre H DEF) (hA : OnCircle A ABC) (hB : OnCircle B ABC)
    (hC : OnCircle C ABC) (hD : OnCircle D DEF) (hE : OnCircle E DEF)
    (hF : OnCircle F DEF) (hAK : OppositeSidesOf A K B C) (hDL : OppositeSidesOf D L E F) :
    (OppositeSidesOf G K B C → OppositeSidesOf H L E F → ∠ B G C = ∠ E H F →
      circumference ABC B K C = circumference DEF E L F ∧
        Arc.Congruent ⟨ABC, B, C, K⟩ ⟨DEF, E, F, L⟩) ∧
    (∠ B A C = ∠ E D F →
      circumference ABC B K C = circumference DEF E L F ∧
        Arc.Congruent ⟨ABC, B, C, K⟩ ⟨DEF, E, F, L⟩) := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be equal circles, and in them let there be equal angles, namely at the
  -- centres the angles BGC, EHF, and at the circumferences the angles BAC, EDF;
  -- I say that the circumference BKC is equal to the circumference ELF.
  -- For let BC, EF be joined.
  have hBCA : Triangle B C A := hAK.triangle
  have hEFD : Triangle E F D := hDL.triangle
  -- Now, since the circles ABC, DEF are equal,
  -- the radii are equal.
  have hGB : ‖G B‖ = ‖H E‖ := hcircles.radii hG hH hB hE
  have hGC : ‖G C‖ = ‖H F‖ := hcircles.radii hG hH hC hF
  -- Thus the two straight lines BG, GC are equal to the two straight lines EH, HF;
  -- and the angle at G is equal to the angle at H;
  -- therefore the base BC is equal to the base EF. [I. 4]
  have base : Triangle G B C → Triangle H E F → ∠ B G C = ∠ E H F → ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ :=
    fun hGBC hHEF h => (BookI.Prop4 hGBC hHEF hGB hGC h).1
  /- When the angles are given at A and D, we sort them into Heath's three cases, acute,
     right and obtuse, as in III.24 (`Prop24.angle_type`), and take each in turn. -/
  have base' : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F → ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ := by
    intro h
    rcases Prop24.angle_type hG hB hC hA hBCA with ⟨hGA, hlt⟩ | ⟨hBGC, hrt⟩ | ⟨hGA, hgt⟩ <;>
      rcases Prop24.angle_type hH hE hF hD hEFD with ⟨hHD, hlt'⟩ | ⟨hEHF, hrt'⟩ | ⟨hHD, hgt'⟩
    · exact base hGA.triangle.cab hHD.triangle.cab
        (by rw [Prop20 hG hA hB hC hGA, Prop20 hH hD hE hF hHD, h])
    · rw [h, hrt'] at hlt; exact absurd hlt (lt_irrefl _)
    · rw [h] at hlt; exact absurd (lt_trans hlt hgt') (lt_irrefl _)
    · rw [← h, hrt] at hlt'; exact absurd hlt' (lt_irrefl _)
    · rw [← len_add_of_between hBGC, ← len_add_of_between hEHF, len_symm B G, hGB, hGC,
        len_symm E H]
    · rw [← h, hrt] at hgt'; exact absurd hgt' (lt_irrefl _)
    · rw [h] at hgt; exact absurd (lt_trans hlt' hgt) (lt_irrefl _)
    · rw [h, hrt'] at hgt; exact absurd hgt (lt_irrefl _)
    · obtain ⟨X, hX, hXG⟩ := exists_onCircle_sameSideOf hB hC hGA.triangle
      obtain ⟨Y, hY, hYH⟩ := exists_onCircle_sameSideOf hE hF hHD.triangle
      have hXA : OppositeSidesOf X A B C := hXG.trans_opposite hGA
      have hYD : OppositeSidesOf Y D E F := hYH.trans_opposite hHD
      have q₁ : ∠ B A C + ∠ B X C = ∟ + ∟ := by
        have := (Prop22 ⟨G, hG⟩ hA hB hX hC hXA.symm).2
        rwa [angle_symm hXA.triangle.ne₂₃ hXA.triangle.ne₁₃] at this
      have q₂ : ∠ E D F + ∠ E Y F = ∟ + ∟ := by
        have := (Prop22 ⟨H, hH⟩ hD hE hY hF hYD.symm).2
        rwa [angle_symm hYD.triangle.ne₂₃ hYD.triangle.ne₁₃] at this
      have hXY : ∠ B X C = ∠ E Y F :=
        CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ B A C) (d := ∠ E D F)
          (by rw [add_comm (∠ B X C), q₁, add_comm (∠ E Y F), q₂]) h
      exact base hGA.triangle.cab hHD.triangle.cab
        (by rw [Prop20 hG hX hB hC hXG.symm, Prop20 hH hY hE hF hYH.symm, hXY])
  -- And, since the angle at A is equal to the angle at D,
  /- When the angles are given at the centres, the angles at A and D are their halves by
     III.20, and so equal. -/
  have atA : OppositeSidesOf G K B C → OppositeSidesOf H L E F → ∠ B G C = ∠ E H F →
      ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F := by
    intro hGK hHL h
    have h1 := Prop20 hG hA hB hC (OppositeSidesOf.sameSideOf hGK.symm hAK.symm)
    have h2 := Prop20 hH hD hE hF (OppositeSidesOf.sameSideOf hHL.symm hDL.symm)
    exact Magnitude.eq_of_add_self_eq (h1.symm.trans (h.trans h2))
  -- the segment BAC is similar to the segment EDF; [III. Def. 11]
  -- and they are upon equal straight lines.
  -- But similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one
  -- another; [III. 24]
  -- therefore the segment BAC is equal to EDF.
  have seg : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ → ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F →
      Arc.Congruent ⟨ABC, B, C, A⟩ ⟨DEF, E, F, D⟩ :=
    fun hBC h => Prop24 ⟨G, hG⟩ ⟨H, hH⟩ hB hC hA hE hF hD hBCA hEFD hBC h
  /- So their circumferences are equal in measure (`Prop24.equalMeasure`). -/
  have hBAC : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ → ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F →
      circumference ABC B A C = circumference DEF E D F :=
    fun hBC h => Prop24.equalMeasure (a := ⟨ABC, B, C, A⟩) (b := ⟨DEF, E, F, D⟩)
      ⟨⟨G, hG⟩, hB, hC, hBCA⟩
      ⟨⟨H, hH⟩, hE, hF, hEFD⟩ (seg hBC h)
  -- But the whole circle ABC is also equal to the whole circle DEF;
  have w₁ := Circumference.whole ⟨G, hG⟩ hB hC hAK
  have w₂ := Circumference.whole ⟨H, hH⟩ hE hF hDL
  -- therefore the circumference BKC which remains is equal to the circumference ELF.
  have rest : ‖B C‖ = ‖E F‖ → ∠ B A C = ∠ E D F →
      circumference ABC B K C = circumference DEF E L F ∧
        Arc.Congruent ⟨ABC, B, C, K⟩ ⟨DEF, E, F, L⟩ := by
    intro hBC hAD
    have hKL : circumference ABC B K C = circumference DEF E L F :=
      CommonNotion3 (w₁.trans w₂.symm) (hBAC hBC hAD)
    /- Their congruence cannot come by subtraction, and comes from III.24 itself. At points
       X, Y of the circles on the sides of K and L, the angles make two right angles with
       the equal angles at A and D [III. 22], so they are equal, and the remaining segments
       are similar; on the equal bases BC, EF they are congruent [III. 24]. Only the side
       names a segment, so they are the segments on the sides of K and L
       (`Arc.Congruent.congr_side`). -/
    obtain ⟨X, hX, hXK⟩ := exists_onCircle_sameSideOf hB hC hAK.symm.triangle
    obtain ⟨Y, hY, hYL⟩ := exists_onCircle_sameSideOf hE hF hDL.symm.triangle
    have hXA : OppositeSidesOf X A B C := hXK.trans_opposite hAK.symm
    have hYD : OppositeSidesOf Y D E F := hYL.trans_opposite hDL.symm
    have hAX : ∠ B A C + ∠ B X C = ∟ + ∟ := by
      have hAX := (Prop22 ⟨G, hG⟩ hA hB hX hC hXA.symm).2
      rwa [angle_symm hXA.triangle.ne₂₃ hXA.triangle.ne₁₃] at hAX
    have hDY : ∠ E D F + ∠ E Y F = ∟ + ∟ := by
      have hDY := (Prop22 ⟨H, hH⟩ hD hE hY hF hYD.symm).2
      rwa [angle_symm hYD.triangle.ne₂₃ hYD.triangle.ne₁₃] at hDY
    have hXY : ∠ B X C = ∠ E Y F :=
      CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ B A C) (d := ∠ E D F)
        (by rw [add_comm (∠ B X C), hAX, add_comm (∠ E Y F), hDY]) hAD
    have hBXC := Prop24 ⟨G, hG⟩ ⟨H, hH⟩ hB hC hX hE hF hY
      hXK.triangle hYL.triangle hBC hXY
    exact ⟨hKL, hBXC.congr_side hXK hYL⟩
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨fun hGK hHL h => rest (base hGK.triangle.cab hHL.triangle.cab h) (atA hGK hHL h),
    fun h => rest (base' h) h⟩
  -- Q. E. D.
```

```lean
/-- The check: the equal measures alone, in each clause, follow from `Prop26` by the first
conjunct of each (checked by Lean). -/
example {A B C D E F G H K L : Point} {ABC DEF : Circle} (hcircles : EqualCircles ABC DEF)
    (hG : Centre G ABC) (hH : Centre H DEF) (hA : OnCircle A ABC) (hB : OnCircle B ABC)
    (hC : OnCircle C ABC) (hD : OnCircle D DEF) (hE : OnCircle E DEF)
    (hF : OnCircle F DEF) (hAK : OppositeSidesOf A K B C) (hDL : OppositeSidesOf D L E F) :
    (OppositeSidesOf G K B C → OppositeSidesOf H L E F → ∠ B G C = ∠ E H F →
      circumference ABC B K C = circumference DEF E L F) ∧
    (∠ B A C = ∠ E D F → circumference ABC B K C = circumference DEF E L F) :=
  ⟨fun hGK hHL h => ((Prop26 hcircles hG hH hA hB hC hD hE hF hAK hDL).1 hGK hHL h).1,
    fun h => ((Prop26 hcircles hG hH hA hB hC hD hE hF hAK hDL).2 h).1⟩
```

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_cases`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L74): Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two. (Between 6)
- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): If B is between A and C, and D is between A and B, then D is between A and C. (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70): If B is between A and C, and C is between B and D, then B is between A and D. (Between 5)
- [`between_of_inside_chord`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L155) (used here): A straight line through a point inside a circle has that point between the points where it meets the circle. (Circle 1)
- [`between_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L43) (used here): If B is between A and C, it is between C and A. (Between 1)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L35) (used here): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`centre_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L32) (used here): A circle has only one centre. (Generalities 2)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L201): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`circles_meet_of_on_inside_outside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L195): Two circles cut one another if the first passes through a point A inside the second, and a point B outside the second is inside or on the first. (Intersection 4, in LeanEuclid's corrected form)
- [`circles_meet_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L81): Two circles that cut one another do so on each side of the straight line through their centres. (Intersections 8)
- [`exists_point`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L26) (used here): Let a point be taken. (Points 1)
- [`exists_point_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L38) (used here): Let a point be taken between B and C. (Points 3)
- [`exists_point_opposite_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L46) (used here): Let a point be taken on the other side of L from B. (Points 6)
- [`inside_not_on`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L38) (used here): A point inside a circle is not on it. (Generalities 4)
- [`inside_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L161) (used here): A circle is "convex": between two points on or inside it, every point is inside. (Circle 2)
- [`line_circle_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L69): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, heading out to a point C outside it, cuts the circle between B and C. (Intersections 4)
- [`line_circle_beyond`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L75) (used here): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, produced beyond B away from C, cuts the circle there. (Intersections 5)
- [`line_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L28) (used here): Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1)
- [`lines_meet_of_opposite_sides`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L179): A straight line joining points on opposite sides of L crosses L. (Intersection 1)
- [`ne_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L46) (used here): A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1)
- [`ne_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L49) (used here): The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L52) (used here): If B is between A and C, then A is not between B and C. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L79): If B is between A and C, and also between A and D, then B is not between C and D: C and D lie on the same side of B. (Between 7)
- [`not_on_line_of_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L92) (used here): Points on one side of a straight line are not on it. (Same side 3)
- [`on_line_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L56): A straight line through A and B, with B between A and C, passes through C. (Between 2)
- [`on_line_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L61) (used here): A straight line through A and C passes through every point between them. (Between 3)
- [`pasch2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L111) (used here): If B is between A and C, A is on L and B is off it, then B and C are on the same side of L: a straight line that leaves L at A does not cross it again. (Pasch 2)
- [`pasch3`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L114) (used here): A straight line through a point between A and C separates them. (Pasch 3)
- [`pasch4`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L119): If two different straight lines L and M meet at B, and A and C are points of M, different from each other and from B, that are not on the same side of L, then B is between A and C. (Pasch 4)
- [`same_side_or`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L99) (used here): A straight line has only two sides. (Same side 5)
- [`same_side_refl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L85): A point off a straight line is on the same side of it as itself. (Same side 1)
- [`same_side_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L89) (used here): If A is on the same side of a straight line as B, then B is on the same side as A. (Same side 2)
- [`same_side_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L96) (used here): Two points on the same side of a straight line as a third point are on the same side as each other. (Same side 4)
- [`triple_incidence1`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L131): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A. If C lies within the angle BAD (on D's side of L and on B's side of N), then B and D are not on the same side of M: the straight line AC separates them. (Triple incidence 1)
- [`triple_incidence2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L139): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A, with B other than A and D off M. If C and D are on the same side of L, and B and D are not on the same side of M, then B and C are on the same side of N: C lies within the angle BAD. (Triple incidence 2)

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`angle_add_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L54) (used here): If D lies within the angle BAC, then BAC is made up of BAD and DAC. (Diagram-angle 2)
- [`angle_eq_of_same_rays`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L72) (used here): The angle doesn't change if its arms are traced through other points on the same rays. (Diagram-angle 4)
- [`angle_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L26) (used here): The angle ABC is the angle CBA. (Metric 4)
- [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L43): Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent. (Metric 9)
- [`area_rotate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L35): The triangle ABC is the triangle CAB. (Metric 8)
- [`area_swap`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L38): The triangle ABC is the triangle ACB. (Metric 8)
- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`inside_of_len_lt`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L33): A point nearer the centre than the circumference is inside. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L21) (used here): If B is between A and C, then AB and BC together make up AC. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_lt_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L37): A point inside is nearer the centre than the circumference. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "straight line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23) (used here): The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L49) (used here): If the angle BAC is nothing, C lies on the ray from A through B. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30): **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L where H is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L23) (used here): Adding three magnitudes in a row, it makes no difference whether the first two or the last two are added first. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26) (used here): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45) (used here): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32) (used here): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35) (used here): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39) (used here): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42) (used here): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**"The circumference BKC which remains."** Euclid has just shown, in III.24, when two segments are equal, and here he puts it to work. The circumference BKC is what remains when the segment BAC is taken from the whole circle, so equal segments in equal circles leave equal circumferences. We read "equal circumferences" as equal in measure and congruent, which says more than Heath's words. The measures go Euclid's way, whole minus part. A congruence cannot be subtracted, so that of the remainders comes from III.24 again: the remaining segments are similar, their angles making two right angles with the equal angles at A and D (III.22).

**Where do the equal circles do their work?** In Euclid's proof, at once, in "the radii are equal": with the equal angles at G and H, I.4 makes BC equal to EF, and III.24 then has its similar segments on equal straight lines. In unequal circles the same angles stand on unequal straight lines, and the segments, though similar, are not equal. Our statement needs them too: a circumference is measured by twice an angle, which carries no radius, so equal angles give equal measures in any two circles, but congruent circumferences only in equal ones. It takes Euclid's two cases one at a time, so where the angles are given at the centres, III.20 halves them for A and D.

**An angle too large for the figure.** Heath writes: "As in III. 21, if Euclid's proof is to cover all cases, it requires us to take cognisance of 'angles at the centre' which are equal to or greater than two right angles. Otherwise we must deal separately with the cases where the angle at the circumference is equal to or greater than a right angle" (vol. 2, p. 57). Our angles are never straight or reflex, so we take his separate cases, sorted as in III.24. If the angle at A is acute, III.20 doubles it at the centre; if right, BC and EF are diameters, each two radii; if obtuse, III.22 passes to the acute angle in the other segment, as Heath proposes.

**The modern way.** In radians, an arc whose angle at the centre is θ, in a circle of radius r, has length rθ, and every angle at the circumference standing on it is θ/2. So in circles of equal radius, equal angles at the centres, or at the circumferences, cut off arcs of equal length, and a rigid motion carries the one onto the other.

## Further reading

- For Euclid joining two of our theorems in one, "thus making the proposition doubly hard for a beginner", where our statement takes his cases one at a time, David Eugene Smith's [*The Teaching of Geometry*](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/37681) (1911, free online), ch. XV (p. 201) (also on [III.14](14.md)).
- For the radian of the modern way, in which an angle is measured by the arc it stands on, Eli Maor's [*Trigonometric Delights*](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691202198/trigonometric-delights) (1998), a warm, story-filled history of trigonometry.
